comment: How-to-test hints for findings whose evidence carries no 'Try:' of its own (0.56.0). FindingHints returns the hint of the FIRST entry whose 'match' is a case-insensitive substring of the finding type -- order specific entries before generic ones. Shown at display/export time only; never written into evidence or state. Plain substrings, no regex.

hints.hint: send Origin: https://attacker.example with your session -- if ACAO echoes it with credentials, a cross-site page can read this response (PoC with fetch(..., {credentials:'include'}))
browsers block * with credentials, but check whether a specific Origin is reflected instead when you send one
request with two different Origin values through any cache/CDN -- a cached reflected ACAO can be served to another origin
try Origin: null, attacker.example, and look-alikes (target.com.attacker.example) -- then check whether credentials are allowed
send a custom Origin and see what ACAO/ACAC come back; only a credentialed reflection is exploitable
any HTML injection on this page becomes script execution -- pair it with reflected/stored input
eval-based gadgets (template engines, setTimeout(string)) are not blocked -- look for DOM sinks fed by input
load script from any host the wildcard allows (CDNs with user uploads / JSONP endpoints) to bypass CSP
frame the page from another origin to test clickjacking on state-changing actions
object/embed injection is not restricted -- relevant only alongside an HTML injection point
if it is a session cookie, any XSS can steal it via document.cookie -- confirm which cookie carries the session
the cookie can travel over plain HTTP -- check whether the site is reachable over http:// or has mixed content
browser default is Lax; test CSRF on top-level GET/POST navigations that change state
request it via any proxy/CDN and from a second session -- check whether another user's data comes back cached
the HTTP subresource can be tampered with on the network; check whether it is script (active) or image (passive)
the secret leaks via logs, Referer and history -- check whether it is still valid and what it grants
set the parameter to https://attacker.example, //attacker.example and /\attacker.example and follow the redirect; chain with OAuth redirect_uri
send a unique marker with < > " ' and see which survive unencoded in that response context, then use the XSS cheatsheet
download it and look for credentials, internal hosts, or (for .git) rebuild the source with git-dumper
download it and diff against the live file -- backups often hold source code or credentials
import the spec into Burp/Postman and call every operation -- especially ones the UI never uses -- with low-priv and no session
dump the schema (InQL / GraphQL Voyager), then test field-level authz, mutations the UI never calls, and query batching
send an introspection query; if disabled, try field suggestions ('Did you mean') to rebuild the schema
fetch the .map and restore the original sources (sourcemapper / browser devtools) -- grep them for routes, keys and comments
low impact on its own -- note it for the report and pair with XSS / clickjacking findings
trigger the error again with malformed input to map framework, versions and internal paths; look for injection points
trigger the error again with malformed input to map framework, versions and internal paths
trigger the error again with malformed input to map framework, versions and internal paths
vary the input that caused it (quotes, types, lengths) -- an SQL/template error is an injection lead
browse the listing for backups, configs and uploads
look for an interactive console or verbose error page (Werkzeug/Django/Laravel debug) -- may allow code execution
use the path for traversal/LFI payloads and to fingerprint the deployment
internal address -- an SSRF target candidate; note which service it belongs to
check anonymous list/read/write on the bucket (aws s3 ls --no-sign-request / az / gsutil)
check anonymous list/read on the container (?restype=container&comp=list)
check anonymous list/read/write on the bucket
tamper with the role/flag in requests and in client-side state to test privilege escalation
flip the flag in the request body/JSON and replay -- mass assignment / privilege escalation
tamper with the role value in requests and replay with a low-priv session
change the level in requests and replay with a low-priv session
decode it (right-click > JWT decode): try alg=none, an empty/weak HMAC secret, kid/jku injection, and an expired token replay
identify what the key signs/decrypts (TLS, JWT, SSH) -- treat as critical and do not use it beyond verification
decode the credentials and check where else they are valid
replay the token against other endpoints/hosts and check its lifetime and scope
a working webhook URL lets anyone post into that channel -- verify it is live without spamming
verify validity with a single read-only call to the provider's whoami/scope endpoint -- never use it beyond that
verify validity with a single read-only call (keyhacks) and check its scope / restrictions -- never use it beyond that
personal data exposure: note which endpoint returns it and whether another user's record can be fetched (IDOR)
personal/payment data exposure: check whether other users' data can be fetched (IDOR)
personal data exposure: check whether other users' data can be fetched (IDOR)
harvest for account enumeration / password-reset testing; check whether other users' emails leak
read for credentials, TODOs, internal hosts and disabled features
